opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing to say is that the line between "pure" and "applied" is much blurrier than it looks in a policy document. Almost every piece of mathematics we now call practical started as something people pursued simply because it was beautiful or puzzling. Number theory was, for centuries, the purest of the pure. G. H. Hardy even took a kind of pride in how useless he thought it was. Today it sits underneath public-key cryptography, which secures essentially every online transaction. Non-Euclidean geometry looked like an abstract curiosity until general relativity needed it. You can't schedule those breakthroughs. You can only make sure the foundation exists when someone needs it.

The second point is about timescales. Policymakers are often working on horizons of a few years, while mathematical ideas can take decades, sometimes a century, to find their application. If you only fund what you can already see a use for, you're essentially living off the intellectual capital previous generations built, and you stop replenishing it. That's a quiet kind of decline. You don't notice it until suddenly you're missing the tools you need.

Third, pure mathematics trains people. The habit of mind it builds, which is holding a very abstract structure in your head, being completely rigorous, and not accepting an argument until it's actually airtight, transfers everywhere. A lot of the people building today's AI systems, financial models, and engineering tools were trained by working on problems that had no obvious application. The funding isn't just buying theorems. It's buying a pipeline of people who can think that way.

And I'd add something that matters to me personally right now. With AI, we're entering a period where formal reasoning and verification are becoming practically important in a very direct way. Can we prove that a piece of software does what it claims? Can we check that an AI system's reasoning is actually correct? Those questions push you straight back into logic, proof theory, and the kind of structural thinking that pure mathematicians have cultivated for a long time. So in a sense, the "useless" part of mathematics is becoming the part we most urgently need.

Finally, I don't think we should be shy about the cultural argument. Mathematics is one of humanity's great achievements, like music or literature. It's a shared body of truth that people across every country and era have contributed to. A society that only values what pays off next quarter is a poorer society. So I'd say pure mathematics deserves funding both because it eventually turns out to be useful, often enormously so, and because understanding for its own sake is worth something in its own right.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the honest answer is that the distinction between "pure" and "applied" is mostly a statement about timing, not about value. Almost every piece of mathematics that now runs the modern world looked completely useless when it was created. Number theory was the classic example of something mathematicians were proud of precisely because it had no applications, and then it became the foundation of all of cryptography, which means every bank transfer and every encrypted message. Group theory, differential geometry, Fourier analysis, linear algebra over huge dimensions: all of these sat around as abstract curiosities for decades or centuries before physics, signal processing, or machine learning suddenly needed exactly that tool.

So when a policymaker says "fund what's practical," the problem is that nobody can actually predict which abstract idea will be practical in thirty years. You can't commission the application-ready version in advance, because the whole point is that the connection is unknown when the work is done. If you only fund things with a visible use case, you're essentially only funding the last mile and hoping someone else built the road.

There's also a second argument that I think gets underrated, which is that pure mathematics is where we train a very specific kind of thinking. Learning to work with objects you can't see, to build long rigorous chains of reasoning, to recognize when two problems that look completely different are secretly the same, that skill transfers everywhere. A lot of the people building AI systems, designing financial models, or doing cryptographic engineering came through that training. Even when the theorems themselves never leave the paper, the people do.

And I'd add something from my own experience working on AI for mathematics. One reason this area is exciting right now is that mathematics is one of the few domains where truth is verifiable. A proof is either correct or it isn't. That makes it an extraordinary testbed for building reasoning systems, and it's only possible because generations of pure mathematicians built this enormous, precise, structured body of knowledge without anyone asking them what it was for.

So my view is that funding pure mathematics isn't charity for an ivory tower. It's one of the cheapest long-term investments a society can make, because the cost is tiny compared to almost any applied program, and the upside, when it hits, reshapes entire industries. The mistake is treating it as a line item that has to justify itself on a five-year horizon. Mathematics doesn't work on that horizon, and the history is very clear that we're better off not forcing it to.

astra-6.text:
I think the premise that pure mathematics and practical applications are competing priorities is a little misleading. Pure mathematics develops ideas that applications can eventually draw on, but that process is difficult to predict. If we only fund research whose usefulness we can explain today, we limit ourselves to the possibilities we already understand.

Number theory is a familiar example: questions about prime numbers can seem very far removed from everyday life, yet they became central to modern cryptography. That doesn’t mean every abstract question will produce a technology, and I wouldn’t justify funding by promising that it will.

There’s also value in understanding something deeply, and in training people to reason carefully about difficult problems. Those are public goods, even when they don’t immediately become products.

Of course, resources are finite, and policymakers should ask what research funding achieves. But I think a healthy research system needs a portfolio: work that addresses immediate needs, and work that expands what we might be able to do decades from now. Pure mathematics deserves a place in that longer-term commitment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think pure mathematics deserves continued funding partly because we can’t reliably predict which ideas will become useful. Research driven by curiosity can develop concepts that, much later, turn out to be exactly what someone needs to solve a practical problem. If we fund only work with an obvious application today, we narrow the possibilities available tomorrow.

But I wouldn’t make the case only in terms of eventual applications. Understanding mathematical structures is itself a valuable human endeavor, much like understanding the universe or creating art. It also trains people to reason carefully, question assumptions, and work through difficult problems.

Policymakers do have to make choices with limited resources. I think the argument is for a balanced research ecosystem: support work that addresses immediate needs, while preserving room for fundamental inquiry whose value may take longer to emerge.
